commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

content.text:
**Tally**

For thirty-one years, Agnes Corrigan climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps of the Harrow Point light every evening, trimmed the wick, wound the clockwork, and watched the lamp swing its white arm across the water. Each morning, once the lamp was dimmed and the logbook filled in with weather and visibility, she went down the rocks to the tideline and looked for glass.

Nobody on the mainland understood it. Her sister wrote asking whether she had considered something with more people in it. Pell, who ran the supply boat every second Thursday with diesel and tinned peaches, once asked if she was hunting treasure.

"Something like that," she said. "Bottles break. Most of what goes into the sea stays sharp for a long time. Once in a while you find a piece that's been worked by the water for twenty years. Blue, white, and now and then a green so pale it looks like breath on a window." She shrugged. "It takes patience to make something smooth."

Pell thought she was a little mad, but he had seen the jars: forty-odd mason jars along the watch room sill, each with a paper label in her cramped handwriting. *Eastern cove, 1994. Storm week. Cobalt, four pieces.* They were the only things in the lighthouse that belonged to her rather than the Service.

In the spring, the Service decided to automate Harrow Point. A sensor array and a solar panel would do the work of her hands. The letter gave a date, the last day of November, and a reassignment to a brick house at Dunmore with a view of a car park.

She did not cry about it. She made a list instead. Things to take: the logbook, the brass sextant, her mother's wool coat. Things to leave: the cot, the kettle, the bad chair. Jars: she stood in front of them a long time and could not decide.

The storm came in the last week of October. It had been building for two days, a bruised color over the western swell, and the barometer dropped so fast the needle seemed to fall off the dial. She lit the lamp early. Through the glass she watched waves climb the lower rocks and break white against the base of the tower, close enough to feel in the iron under her boots.

She stayed awake all night, logging wind speeds with numb fingers. Near four in the morning the radio crackled: the fishing boat *Mary Ellen* needed a bearing. Agnes gave it. The boat came around the reef by the light she had kept burning for three decades, and at dawn its running lamps bobbed past the point. A man on deck raised a hand toward the tower. She raised one back.

When the storm broke, the sea had shifted everything. The high-tide line was strewn with kelp and driftwood and the things the water had been keeping. She went down anyway.

The beach was unrecognizable. The rocks at the north end, which she had combed for years, were buried under a fan of sand. She worked slowly, pushing back weed with a gloved hand. Near the foot of the cliff, wedged between two stones, she found a piece of glass the size of a thumbnail: deep, clear blue, its edges rounded to the softness of an old doorstep.

She turned it over. The frosting was perfect. It had come from some bottle broken off a ship or dropped from a deck decades ago, and it had tumbled in the surf for years before the sea finally let it go to her.

She sat on the wet rock and held it for a while.

That afternoon, when she climbed back up, she did not put the piece in a jar. She set it on the sill beside the logbook and wrote a new label. *Harrow Point. Last storm. One piece, blue.* Then she sat in the bad chair and watched the light turn overhead, beginning its routine for the last time.

In November, Pell brought the supply boat in and carried the boxes down the tower himself. She had packed forty-two jars in straw and newspaper. The blue piece she had kept back for her pocket.

"You're taking all of them?" Pell asked.

"All of them."

He looked up at the tower, then at her. "Think they'll let you keep a light somewhere else?"

"No," she said. "But I can keep a tally."

The boat pulled away. Behind her, the lamp blinked on at the top of the tower, steady and white, though no one would climb the steps to trim its wick anymore. It swept the water and guided ships around the reef, as it always had.

In her coat pocket, the blue piece knocked softly against her hip, worn smooth by the sea and by her hand.
